\title{Few-Shot Direction Calibration of Relational and Attribute Statistics for Training-Free Graph Anomaly Detection}

\abstract{Training-free graph anomaly detectors score nodes with relational statistics and must decide, for each statistic, whether high or low values are anomalous. We show that this direction decides their performance and that its sign cannot be learned without labels: unlabelled data are consistent with anomalies in either tail, labelled normal nodes carry little information when anomalies are rare, and for any statistic whose anomalies are separated from the graph by a nonzero margin, a few labelled anomalies identify which tail is anomalous with an error that falls exponentially in their number at a rate set by that margin. Building on these results, we propose few-shot direction calibration (FDC), a training-free method that orients and weights relational and attribute statistics using only $k$ labelled anomalies. We evaluate FDC on 16 development graphs and, after freezing the method, on four held-out graphs, against the official GDN and BWGNN given the same labels. On the development graphs FDC reaches a mean AUROC of 0.800 with ten labelled anomalies (GDN 0.645, BWGNN 0.527). On every held-out graph it has a higher AUROC than both baselines (mean 0.723 against 0.525 and 0.491; graph-level difference to GDN $+0.17$, 95\% bootstrap interval [0.07, 0.32]), also when they receive a labelled validation set; with four graphs this is a pre-specified transfer check rather than a high-powered test. In AUROC, FDC also beats the best single calibrated statistic and shot-similarity baselines and is insensitive to its settings, but on one held-out graph pooling lowers precision at the top of the ranking. All protocols were fixed before the corresponding results were seen.}

\keywords{Graph anomaly detection, Few-shot learning, Training-free detection, Identifiability, Positive-unlabelled learning, Pre-registration}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}

Graph anomaly detection (GAD) identifies nodes whose attributes, connections, or both are unusual relative to the rest of a graph \citep{akoglu2015graph,ma2023comprehensive}. It is used to find fraudulent reviewers, spam accounts and compromised nodes, where labels are scarce and expensive. Most detectors learn a representation of each target graph, by reconstruction \citep{ding2019deep}, contrastive learning \citep{liu2021cola} or affinity maximisation \citep{qiao2023truncated}. Generalist detectors train once on source graphs and transfer to new ones \citep{niu2025unprompt,qiao2025anomalygfm,liu2024arc}. Training-free detectors avoid training altogether and score nodes with relational statistics computed directly on the target graph \citep{zhao2025freegad,wei2026neighbordiv}.

Training-free detectors are cheap, transparent and need no source data. They also rest on a choice that is rarely stated: for every statistic, someone must decide which tail is anomalous. A node whose features disagree with its neighbours is usually suspicious, so neighbour disagreement is scored in its upper tail; a node embedded in few triangles may be suspicious, so triangle participation is scored in its lower tail. These directions are set once and applied to every graph.

We found that these directions decide performance. Our own nine-statistic training-free detector, CoRe-GAD-MSDA, performed well on the graphs it was developed on, reproduced exactly, and still fell below random on several standard benchmarks. The cause was orientation. On graphs with injected clique anomalies, anomalous nodes have \emph{many} triangles, not few; on Weibo, Tolokers and YelpChi, anomalous accounts are \emph{more} similar to their neighbours than normal accounts are. Sixteen label-free rules for choosing directions per graph, fixed in a pre-registered protocol, all failed to generalise, and so did directions chosen from labelled normal nodes. Only labelled anomalies recovered the direction reliably.

This paper turns that observation into a method and explains why it works. Our contributions are as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Theory.} We prove that the anomalous direction of a statistic is not identified by unlabelled data, that $m'$ labelled normal nodes leave it undetermined with probability of order $\exp(-m'\pi/(1-\pi))$ when the anomaly rate is $\pi$, and that $k$ labelled anomalies identify it with error at most $\exp(-2k\Delta^2)$, where $\Delta$ is the separation of the statistic, with a corresponding bound for the choice among upper, lower and two-sided tails (Section~\ref{sec:theory}). The results hold for any fixed graph, without a distributional model.
\item \textbf{Method.} We propose few-shot direction calibration (FDC), which orients and weights relational and attribute statistics using only $k$ labelled anomalies and the unlabelled graph, with no training (Section~\ref{sec:method}). Its weight threshold is a per-statistic noise floor derived from the null distribution of the shots (Section~\ref{sec:theory}), and its use of attribute statistics is gated by the number of shots.
\item \textbf{Evaluation.} We compare FDC with the official code of GDN \citep{ding2021few} and BWGNN \citep{tang2022rethinking} under identical supervision on 16 development graphs, and then on four held-out graphs after freezing the method (Sections~\ref{sec:setup}--\ref{sec:results}). Every protocol and selection rule was fixed and hashed before the corresponding results were computed, and the development history of the method is reported in full. Significance is assessed with the graph as the unit of analysis, and we add lightweight baselines, a null experiment and sensitivity analyses.
\end{enumerate}

FDC has the higher AUROC than both baselines on all four held-out graphs and on 11 to 12 of 15--16 development graphs at each shot size; at the graph level its advantage over GDN and BWGNN is significant on the development graphs, while the four held-out graphs give a consistent effect but too few graphs for significance. It is weaker on some organic-anomaly graphs (Questions, Tolokers) and on Facebook, where the official GDN is nearly perfect. We report these cases, a loss in normalised AP and R-precision on the held-out graphs relative to the relational-only variant and the best single statistic, and the fact that FDC is not faster than GDN, whose official model is a small linear network.

\section{Related work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Unsupervised and generalist GAD.} Early detectors used ego-network statistics and residual models \citep{10.1007/978-3-642-13672-6_40,ijcai2017p299}. Deep unsupervised detectors reconstruct attributes and structure \citep{ding2019deep}, contrast nodes with their neighbourhoods \citep{liu2021cola,jin2021anemone,zheng2023slgad}, or maximise local affinity \citep{qiao2023truncated,zhang2025gctam}; surveys organise these families \citep{ma2023comprehensive,11048498}. Generalist detectors transfer across graphs: UNPrompt with neighbourhood prompts \citep{niu2025unprompt}, AnomalyGFM with normal and abnormal prototypes \citep{qiao2025anomalygfm}, ARC with in-context learning \citep{liu2024arc}, and ReFi-GAD with relational fingerprints \citep{liu2026refigad}. In their few-shot modes, ARC and AnomalyGFM receive labelled \emph{normal} nodes of the target graph. FreeGAD and NeighborDiv remove training and score nodes with fixed-sign deviations \citep{zhao2025freegad,wei2026neighbordiv}; the orientation problem studied here applies to them directly.

\paragraph{Few-shot and semi-supervised GAD with labelled anomalies.} Deviation networks learn anomaly scores from a few labelled anomalies and unlabelled data by pushing the labelled anomalies away from a Gaussian reference \citep{pang2019deep}. GDN brings this idea to graphs, and Meta-GDN adds meta-learning across auxiliary graphs that share the target's feature space \citep{ding2021few}. Spectral GNNs such as BWGNN are strong supervised detectors when many labels are available \citep{tang2022rethinking}; GADBench compares such detectors in fully and semi-supervised settings \citep{tang2023gadbench}. Our setting, a few labelled anomalies and no labelled normal nodes, is positive--unlabelled learning \citep{elkan2008learning,bekker2020learning}; unlike these methods, FDC has no trainable parameters and uses the labels only to orient and weight a fixed set of statistics.

\paragraph{Evaluation practice.} Evaluation studies in outlier detection have shown that conclusions depend strongly on datasets, measures and protocols \citep{campos2016evaluation,3600270.3602229,tang2023gadbench}. Negative results are under-reported in machine learning \citep{karl2024negative}, and pre-registration guards against analyses tuned after seeing results \citep{nosek2018preregistration}. For comparisons over many datasets we follow \citet{demsar2006statistical} and test over datasets rather than over runs, with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test \citep{wilcoxon1945individual} or, for very few datasets, the sign test.

\section{Base detector}\label{sec:detector}

FDC is built on CoRe-GAD-MSDA, a training-free detector developed by the authors and not published elsewhere. Its name refers to its calibrated relational (CoRe) evidence and its multi-statistic direction-aware (MSDA) scoring. Fig.~\ref{fig:detector} gives an overview; we specify the detector fully because FDC changes only its orientation and weighting steps.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig/Fig1_detector.pdf}
\caption{Overview of the base detector CoRe-GAD-MSDA. Nine statistics are computed per node, calibrated as signed empirical ranks against a reference set that excludes the query and its neighbours, oriented by a tail direction, and fused with label-free reliability weights and a contextual/structural branch maximum. FDC (Section~\ref{sec:method}) replaces the fixed orientation with one calibrated from labelled anomalies and adds attribute statistics.}
\label{fig:detector}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Setting and preprocessing.} Let $\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathbf{X})$ be an undirected attributed graph with $n$ nodes, binary adjacency matrix $\mathbf{A}$ without self-loops, degree matrix $\mathbf{D}$ and features $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$; $\mathcal{N}_i$ and $d_i=|\mathcal{N}_i|$ are the neighbours and degree of node $v_i$. Non-finite feature entries are replaced by their column median, constant columns are removed, each column is standardised and each row is scaled to unit norm. We write $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i$ for the result and $\delta_{uv}=1-\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_u^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_v$ for the cosine dissimilarity of two nodes.

\paragraph{Relational statistics.} For each node the detector computes nine statistics (Table~\ref{tab:stats}). To bound cost, $\widehat{\mathcal{N}}_i$ is $\mathcal{N}_i$ if $d_i\le q$ and otherwise a uniform sample of $q=32$ neighbours, and $\widehat{\mathcal{P}}_i$ is the set of unordered neighbour pairs if there are at most $L=128$ of them and otherwise a uniform sample of $L$ pairs. The six contextual statistics are
\begin{align}
t_{i1}&=\frac{1}{|\widehat{\mathcal{N}}_i|}\sum_{j\in\widehat{\mathcal{N}}_i}\delta_{ij}, &
t_{i2}&=\frac{1}{|\widehat{\mathcal{P}}_i|}\sum_{(u,v)\in\widehat{\mathcal{P}}_i}\delta_{uv}, \nonumber\\
t_{i3}&=\frac{1}{|\widehat{\mathcal{P}}_i|}\sum_{(u,v)\in\widehat{\mathcal{P}}_i}\big(\delta_{uv}-t_{i2}\big)^2, &
t_{i4}&=\frac{1}{|\widehat{\mathcal{P}}_i|}\sum_{(u,v)\in\widehat{\mathcal{P}}_i}A_{uv}, \nonumber\\
t_{i5}&=\frac{1}{d_i}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_i}\log(1+d_j), &
t_{i6}&=1-\cos\big(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i,\mathbf{h}_i\big),\quad \mathbf{H}=(\mathbf{D}+\mathbf{I})^{-1}(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{I})\tilde{\mathbf{X}}.
\end{align}
With $\mathcal{T}_i$ the neighbour pairs that close a triangle with $v_i$ and $\mathcal{U}_i$ the $\lceil\sqrt{d_i}\rceil$ neighbours with the largest $\delta_{ij}$, the three structural statistics are
\begin{equation}
t_{i7}=\frac{|\mathcal{T}_i|}{d_i}, \qquad
t_{i8}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{U}_i|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{U}_i}\delta_{ij}, \qquad
t_{i9}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_i|}\sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{T}_i}\frac{\delta_{iu}+\delta_{iv}+\delta_{uv}}{3}.
\end{equation}
On dense graphs, triangle counts and motif sums are computed exactly with sparse matrix identities in row blocks.

\paragraph{Isolated nodes and missing values.} A statistic is \emph{missing} for a node when its formula has no terms. For a node of degree $d_i$ this gives the following rules. For $d_i=0$ (an isolated node), $t_{i1}$, $t_{i5}$ and $t_{i8}$ are missing; for $d_i\le1$, $t_{i2}$, $t_{i3}$ and $t_{i4}$ are missing, since there is no neighbour pair; $t_{i9}$ is missing whenever $\mathcal{T}_i=\emptyset$, which includes every node with $d_i\le1$. Two statistics are defined for every node: $t_{i7}$ is set to $0$ when $d_i\le1$ (no triangle can exist), and $t_{i6}$ is defined because $\mathbf{h}_i=\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i$ for an isolated node, giving $t_{i6}=0$ when its feature vector is non-zero. A node whose preprocessed feature vector is zero has cosine similarity $0$ with every node, so $\delta_{uv}=1$ in all its terms. Missing values are never imputed. They are excluded from every reference set $\mathcal{V}_j$, receive $M_{ij}=0$, and therefore contribute neither evidence nor weight in Eqs.~\eqref{eq:orient}--\eqref{eq:fusion}; a node all of whose statistics in a branch are missing scores 0 in that branch.

\begin{table}[!ht]
\caption{Relational statistics of the base detector and their fixed directions (U: upper tail anomalous; L: lower tail; 2: two-sided).}
\label{tab:stats}

Branch & Statistic & Symbol & Fixed direction \\
\midrule
Contextual & Node--neighbour discrepancy & $t_1$ & U \\

\paragraph{Rank calibration.} Let $\mathcal{V}_j$ be the nodes for which statistic $j$ is defined and $\mathcal{R}_{ij}=\mathcal{V}_j\setminus(\{i\}\cup\mathcal{N}_i)$ the reference set of node $i$, of size $m_{ij}$. The neighbourhood-excluded signed midrank is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank}
r_{ij}=\frac{2}{m_{ij}}\Big(\sum_{l\in\mathcal{R}_{ij}}\mathbb{1}[t_{lj}<t_{ij}]+\tfrac12\sum_{l\in\mathcal{R}_{ij}}\mathbb{1}[t_{lj}=t_{ij}]\Big)-1\in[-1,1],
\end{equation}
and $M_{ij}=1$ if $t_{ij}$ is defined and $m_{ij}>0$, else $0$. The graph-wide signed midrank $\bar r_{ij}$ is defined in the same way with $\mathcal{R}_{ij}$ replaced by $\mathcal{V}_j$.

\paragraph{Orientation, weighting and fusion.} A tail direction $\theta_j\in\{\text{upper},\text{lower},\text{two-sided}\}$ turns a rank into evidence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:orient}
e_{ij}=M_{ij}\cdot\begin{cases}(1+r_{ij})/2 & \theta_j=\text{upper},\\ (1-r_{ij})/2 & \theta_j=\text{lower},\\ |r_{ij}| & \theta_j=\text{two-sided}.\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Each coordinate receives a label-free reliability weight $\omega_{ij}=a_{ij}b_jc_{ij}$, the product of a support factor $a_{ij}=M_{ij}\min(1,m_{ij}/\max(n_j^{*}-1,1))$ with $n_j^*=\sum_iM_{ij}$, a dispersion factor $b_j=\min(1,\mathrm{IQR}\{e_{ij}\}/0.5)$, and a stability factor $c_{ij}=M_{ij}\max(0,1-|r_{ij}-\bar r_{ij}|/2)$. The score is the larger of the weighted mean evidence of the contextual statistics ($j\le6$) and of the structural statistics ($j\ge7$),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fusion}
s_i=\max\Big(\frac{\sum_{j\le6}\omega_{ij}e_{ij}}{\sum_{j\le6}\omega_{ij}},\;\frac{\sum_{j\ge7}\omega_{ij}e_{ij}}{\sum_{j\ge7}\omega_{ij}}\Big),
\end{equation}
with an empty branch scoring 0. With the fixed directions of Table~\ref{tab:stats}, the detector needs no labels and has no trainable parameters.

\section{Why fixed or label-free directions fail}\label{sec:motivation}

This section summarises the evidence that motivated FDC. It comes from an earlier study of the base detector on 21 standard benchmark files, which we reproduce here only as far as it is needed.

\paragraph{Reproduction.} The base detector's original results reproduce exactly (164 of 164 released AUROC and AP values), and the official UNPrompt and AnomalyGFM reruns are close to their published values. The failures below are therefore not implementation artefacts.

\subsection{The anomalous direction depends on the anomaly mechanism}\label{sec:rq3}

Fig.~\ref{fig:diag} shows, for each graph and statistic, the AUROC of the oriented statistic on its own. On every graph with injected clique anomalies, triangle load is reversed: planted cliques give anomalous nodes unusually many triangles. On Weibo, Tolokers and YelpChi, the discrepancy statistics and the propagation residual are reversed: anomalous accounts are more similar to their neighbours than normal accounts are, a pattern consistent with camouflage. The same nine statistics that score below random on Weibo with the fixed directions reach 0.824 AUROC when oriented two-sided. No fixed choice of directions works on all graphs.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig/Fig2_direction_diagnostic.pdf}
\caption{AUROC of each statistic of the base detector on its own, in its fixed direction, averaged over five seeds. Blue: the fixed direction separates anomalies; red: it is reversed. Bold values are below 0.45. Motif incoherence is undefined on Reddit, which has no triangles. Appendix~\ref{app:diag} lists the same values in a table.}
\label{fig:diag}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Label-free rules do not generalise}\label{sec:rq4}

Before running them, we fixed 16 rules for choosing each statistic's direction from unlabelled data: two references (fixed directions, all two-sided), twelve rules based on the skewness of each statistic, and two consensus rules that align each statistic with the others. The rule with the best development utility, a consensus rule, was frozen and tested. It improved four untouched graphs but lowered mean AUROC on the other test graphs from 0.672 to 0.616, collapsing on Facebook, Flickr and YelpChi. All twelve skewness rules were below random on average, and a representative skewness rule chose the anomalous direction in only 31\% of decisive cases.

\subsection{Labelled normal nodes do not help; labelled anomalies do}\label{sec:rq5}

Fig.~\ref{fig:recovery} shows how often each source of information chooses the direction in which a statistic actually separates anomalies, over 510 decisive statistic--graph--seed cases. Fixed directions are right in 56\% of cases and the consensus rule in 62\%. A rule using $k$ labelled normal nodes, the supervision of ARC and AnomalyGFM, does not improve with $k$ (59\%, 60\% and 54\% for $k=1,5,10$); with ten normal shots the base detector's mean AUROC on ARC's eight test graphs fell from 0.704 to 0.586. Labelled anomalies behave differently: one labelled anomaly with one normal node already gives 68\%, and ten of each give 75\%. FDC is designed to exploit this asymmetry, and Section~\ref{sec:theory} explains it.

\caption{Share of decisive statistics oriented in their anomalous direction, pooled over graphs and seeds. Only labelled anomalies move the share well above chance.}
\label{fig:recovery}
\end{figure}

\section{When can the anomalous direction be identified?}\label{sec:theory}

This section explains the empirical pattern of Sections~\ref{sec:rq3}--\ref{sec:rq5}: label-free rules fail, labelled normal nodes barely help, and a few labelled anomalies are enough. The results are stated for a single relational or attribute statistic on a fixed graph, so they hold without any distributional model of the graph. Proofs are given in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}.

\subsection{Setting}

Let $G$ be a graph with node set $V$, $|V| = n$, and let $\mathcal{A} \subset V$ be the anomalous nodes, $|\mathcal{A}| = m$, with contamination $\pi = m/n$; $\mathcal{N} = V \setminus \mathcal{A}$ are the normal nodes. A statistic assigns a value $t_i$ to every node. Its \emph{graph-wide rank position} is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rankpos}
U_i \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{l \in V}\Big(\mathbb{1}[t_l < t_i] + \tfrac12\,\mathbb{1}[t_l = t_i]\Big) \in (0,1),
\end{equation}
which equals $(r_i + 1)/2$ for the graph-wide signed midrank $r_i$ used by the detector. Write
\begin{equation}
\mu = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} U_i, \qquad
\mathrm{AUC} = \frac{1}{m\,(n-m)}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}}\sum_{l \in \mathcal{N}}\Big(\mathbb{1}[t_l < t_i] + \tfrac12\,\mathbb{1}[t_l = t_i]\Big),
\end{equation}
so $\mathrm{AUC}$ is the AUROC obtained by scoring nodes with the upper tail of the statistic. The upper tail is the anomalous direction if $\mathrm{AUC} > \tfrac12$ and the lower tail if $\mathrm{AUC} < \tfrac12$.

\begin{lemma}[Direction is the sign of the mean rank position]\label{lem:sign}
$\mu - \tfrac12 = (1-\pi)\,(\mathrm{AUC} - \tfrac12)$. Hence the upper tail is anomalous if and only if $\mu > \tfrac12$, and the \emph{direction margin}
\[ \Delta = |\mu - \tfrac12| = (1-\pi)\,|\mathrm{AUC} - \tfrac12| \]
measures how strongly the statistic separates anomalies in its anomalous direction.
\end{lemma}

The lemma matters because $\mu$ can be estimated from labelled anomalies alone, using the whole unlabelled graph as reference: no labelled normal node is needed.

\subsection{Unlabelled data do not identify the direction}

A \emph{label-free rule} is any procedure, possibly randomised, whose output depends on the graph, its features and the statistics, but not on any label. All 16 rules of Section~\ref{sec:rq4} are of this kind.

\begin{theorem}[Label-free non-identifiability]\label{thm:nonid}
Let the statistic take distinct values and let $1 \le m < n/2$. Let $\mathcal{A}_{\uparrow}$ be the $m$ nodes with the largest values and $\mathcal{A}_{\downarrow}$ the $m$ nodes with the smallest. Labelling $\mathcal{A}_{\uparrow}$ as anomalous gives $\mathrm{AUC} = 1$; labelling $\mathcal{A}_{\downarrow}$ gives $\mathrm{AUC} = 0$. Both labellings have the same contamination and leave the input of every label-free rule unchanged, so every label-free rule chooses the wrong signed direction (upper or lower) with probability at least $\tfrac12$ under one of them.
\end{theorem}

Theorem~\ref{thm:nonid} is elementary, but it fixes what a label-free rule can and cannot do. Skewness, consensus and similar rules succeed only when the unknown labelling mechanism happens to place anomalies in the tail the rule favours. That is an assumption about how anomalies arise, not something the data can confirm. The benchmarks contain both mechanisms: injected clique anomalies sit in the upper tail of triangle statistics, while organic camouflaged anomalies sit in the lower tail of neighbour disagreement (Section~\ref{sec:rq3}). This is why no fixed label-free rule transferred.

\begin{remark}[Scope of Theorem~\ref{thm:nonid}]\label{rem:scope}
The theorem concerns the \emph{signed} direction. It does not say that unlabelled data are useless for detection: two-sided evidence $|r|$ needs no labels and scores both tails. Its cost is that half of its evidence lies in the tail that contains no anomalies, so it ranks the anomalies below every extreme normal node in the other tail. In the earlier study the all-two-sided rule was a reasonable label-free default (mean AUROC 0.66--0.68 across the three splits) but was beaten by correctly signed statistics wherever the direction was stable. FDC therefore keeps the two-sided option and lets the labelled anomalies choose among the three.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Labelled normal nodes are weak evidence}

Labelled normal nodes add information, but very little when anomalies are rare. Suppose $m'$ normal nodes are drawn uniformly without replacement from $\mathcal{N}$ and revealed.

\begin{theorem}[Normal shots]\label{thm:normal}
In the setting of Theorem~\ref{thm:nonid}, assume $n \ge 2m + m'$. Every rule that uses the graph and $m'$ labelled normal nodes chooses the wrong direction, under one of the two labellings, with probability at least
\[
\tfrac12\,q, \qquad
q = \prod_{i=0}^{m'-1}\frac{n-2m-i}{\,n-m-i\,} \;\ge\; \Big(1 - \frac{m}{\,n-m-m'+1\,}\Big)^{m'} \;\approx\; \exp\!\Big(-\frac{m'\pi}{1-\pi}\Big).
\]
\end{theorem}

To push this worst-case error below $\varepsilon$, roughly $m' \ge \frac{1-\pi}{\pi}\ln\frac{1}{2\varepsilon}$ normal nodes are required. With $\pi = 0.05$ and $\varepsilon = 0.1$ this is about 31 labelled normal nodes for a single statistic. With the $m' = 10$ normal shots used by ARC and AnomalyGFM, the bound is between $0.15$ and $0.39$ on the 14 of the 16 development graphs with $\pi < 0.11$. This agrees with the near-chance direction recovery from normal shots reported in Section~\ref{sec:rq5}. The reason is an asymmetry: when anomalies are rare, normal nodes look like the graph as a whole, so they say little about which tail the few anomalies occupy.

\subsection{A few labelled anomalies identify the direction}

Now suppose $k$ anomalies are drawn uniformly without replacement from $\mathcal{A}$ and revealed. The calibration rule estimates $\mu$ by the mean rank position of the shots,
\[
\hat\mu = \frac1k \sum_{s=1}^{k} U_{a_s},
\]
and chooses the upper tail if $\hat\mu > \tfrac12$ and the lower tail otherwise. The mean of $\hat\mu$ is $\mu$, and each $U_{a_s}$ lies in $(0,1)$.

\begin{theorem}[Anomaly shots]\label{thm:anomaly}
Let $\Delta > 0$ be the direction margin of Lemma~\ref{lem:sign} and $\sigma^2 = \frac1m \sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} (U_i - \mu)^2$ the spread of the anomalies' rank positions. The probability that the calibration rule chooses the wrong direction satisfies
\[
\Pr[\text{wrong direction}] \;\le\; \min\left\{ \exp\!\big(-2k\Delta^2\big),\;
\exp\!\left(-\frac{k\Delta^2}{2\sigma^2 + 2\Delta/3}\right)\right\}.
\]
\end{theorem}

Theorem~\ref{thm:anomaly} covers the choice between the two signed directions. FDC chooses among three candidates, the two signed tails and the two-sided evidence, by the largest shot mean. The same argument applies to this three-way choice.

\begin{corollary}[Three-way selection]\label{cor:three}
Let $\mu^{\uparrow}, \mu^{\downarrow}, \mu^{\leftrightarrow}$ be the mean upper, lower and two-sided evidence of the anomalies, let $t^{*}$ be the candidate with the largest mean, and let $g_t = \mu^{t^*} - \mu^{t} > 0$ be its gap to each other candidate $t$. The probability that the largest shot mean belongs to a candidate other than $t^*$ is at most $\sum_{t \ne t^*} \exp(-k g_t^2/2)$. For the two signed tails $g = 2\Delta$, which recovers the Hoeffding term of Theorem~\ref{thm:anomaly}.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[How many anomalies to label]\label{cor:k}
If $J$ statistics all have margin at least $\Delta_{\min}$, all their directions are correct with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ once
\[
k \;\ge\; \frac{\ln(J/\varepsilon)}{2\,\Delta_{\min}^{2}}.
\]
\end{corollary}

The contrast with Theorem~\ref{thm:normal} is sharp. In the two extreme labellings of Theorem~\ref{thm:nonid}, a single labelled anomaly reveals the direction exactly, while $m'$ normal nodes leave it undetermined with probability close to $\exp(-m'\pi/(1-\pi))$. In general the error with anomaly shots decays exponentially in $k$ at a rate set by $\Delta$, which depends on the contamination only through the factor $1-\pi$. With labelled normal nodes, the worst-case rate is throttled by $\pi$ itself.

\subsection{Choosing which statistics to trust}

With few shots, some statistics look separating by chance. The method therefore weights statistic $j$ by $w_j = \max(0,\ \hat s_j - \tau_k)$. Here $\hat s_j$ is the estimated separation of its chosen tail and $\tau_k = 1/\sqrt{12k}$.

\begin{proposition}[Null behaviour of the evidence]\label{prop:tau}
Suppose the $k$ shots are a uniform random sample of nodes with respect to statistic $j$ (no anomaly signal).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For the upper and lower evidence, with or without ties, the shot mean has expectation exactly $\tfrac12$ and standard deviation at most $1/\sqrt{12k} = \tau_k$.
\item[(b)] For the two-sided evidence, the shot mean has expectation $m_j = \frac1n\sum_i |\bar r_{ij}| \le \tfrac12$, with equality up to $O(1/n^2)$ when the values are distinct, and variance $\sigma_{j}^2/k$, where $\sigma_j^2 = \frac1n\sum_i(|\bar r_{ij}| - m_j)^2 \le \tfrac14$. With ties, $m_j$ can be well below $\tfrac12$ and $\sigma_j^2$ can exceed $\tfrac1{12}$.
\item[(c)] If instead statistic $j$ has margin $\Delta_j > \tau_k$, it keeps a positive weight with probability at least $1 - \exp\!\big(-2k(\Delta_j - \tau_k)^2\big)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

For the signed evidence, $\tau_k$ is therefore an upper bound on one null standard deviation of the shot mean, and statistics whose apparent separation lies within it are switched off. For the two-sided evidence the method centres at $\tfrac12 \ge m_j$, which makes retention harder when ties lower $m_j$, but the null spread can exceed $\tau_k$. On our graphs this matters little: across the 143 non-empty statistic--graph pairs of the development set, $\sigma_j^2 \le 0.0843$, at most $1.2\%$ above $\tfrac1{12}$, while heavily tied statistics have $m_j$ as low as $0.28$ (and $0$ for the few statistics that are constant on a graph). The threshold is a per-statistic noise floor, not a guarantee on the number of statistics retained by chance across all $9+2p$ statistics and three candidate directions; Section~\ref{sec:null} measures that number directly with random shots. Finally, the proposition explains why few shots call for caution with many statistics (for $k=1$, a signed statistic with distinct values and no signal passes the threshold with probability $0.42$), but it does not single out $k = 3$ as the point at which to add attribute statistics. That gate was chosen in the last development round (Section~\ref{sec:setup}); Section~\ref{sec:sens} reports the alternatives.

\subsection{Empirical check}

Table~\ref{tab:bound} compares the observed direction error of the calibration rule with Theorem~\ref{thm:anomaly}, using the exact $\Delta$ and $\sigma^2$ of each statistic computed from all labels. It pools 9 relational statistics, 16 development graphs and 5 seeds. The observed error never exceeds either bound. Both bounds are conservative: for margins above $0.2$, no error was observed at $k = 10$, while Hoeffding's bound allows $35\%$ and Bernstein's $16\%$. The variance-adaptive Bernstein bound is the tighter of the two throughout. Statistics with margin below $0.05$ are close to a coin flip at every $k$, as the theory predicts; the weight threshold of Proposition~\ref{prop:tau} is designed to discard exactly these.

\section{Few-shot direction calibration}\label{sec:method}

FDC receives a graph and a set $\mathcal{S}$ of $k$ labelled anomalies; all other nodes are unlabelled. It orients and weights a set of statistics using $\mathcal{S}$ and the graph-wide ranks of Section~\ref{sec:detector}, and it has no trainable parameters. Algorithm~\ref{alg:fdc} summarises it.

\paragraph{Statistics.} FDC uses the nine relational statistics of Section~\ref{sec:detector} and $2p$ attribute statistics, $p=\min(16,d-1)$. Let $\mathbf{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ be a low-dimensional summary of the features: the first $p$ principal components of the column-standardised features when $d\le64$ and at least 30\% of the feature entries are non-zero, and otherwise a truncated singular value decomposition of the row-normalised features. The attribute statistics of node $i$ are its own components $z_{i1},\dots,z_{ip}$ and the mean of its neighbours' components, $\frac{1}{d_i}\sum_{l\in\mathcal{N}_i}z_{l1},\dots$ (zero for isolated nodes). Attribute statistics are valid for every node.

\paragraph{Calibrating a statistic.} For statistic $j$, let $\mathcal{S}_j\subseteq\mathcal{S}$ be the labelled anomalies for which it is defined. Its three candidate separations are the mean graph-wide evidence of these anomalies,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sep}
\hat\mu^{\uparrow}_j=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_j|}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{S}_j}\frac{1+\bar r_{aj}}{2},\qquad
\hat\mu^{\downarrow}_j=1-\hat\mu^{\uparrow}_j,\qquad
\hat\mu^{\leftrightarrow}_j=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_j|}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{S}_j}|\bar r_{aj}|.
\end{equation}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:sign}, $\hat\mu^{\uparrow}_j$ estimates the rank position $\mu$ of the anomalies, so it is an estimate of the statistic's AUROC against the whole graph. FDC sets $\theta_j$ to the tail with the largest estimate (ties go to the fixed direction, or to the upper tail for attribute statistics) and records the estimated separation $\hat s_j=\max(0,\hat\mu^{\theta_j}_j-\tfrac12)$. A statistic with $\mathcal{S}_j=\emptyset$ keeps its default direction and $\hat s_j=0$.

\paragraph{Scoring with few shots ($k<3$).} With one or two labelled anomalies, FDC uses only the relational statistics. It runs the base detector with the calibrated directions $\theta_j$ and multiplies each reliability weight by the estimated separation, $\omega_{ij}\hat s_j$, in Eq.~\eqref{eq:fusion}. We call this relational-only scorer FDC-R.

\paragraph{Scoring with more shots ($k\ge3$).} With three or more labelled anomalies, FDC pools all $9+2p$ statistics and scores each node by the weighted mean of its oriented graph-wide evidence,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fdc}
s_i=\frac{\sum_j w_j\,\bar e_{ij}\,M_{ij}}{\sum_j w_j\,M_{ij}},\qquad w_j=\max\big(0,\ \hat s_j-\tau_k\big),\qquad \tau_k=\frac{1}{\sqrt{12k}},
\end{equation}
where $\bar e_{ij}$ is Eq.~\eqref{eq:orient} applied to $\bar r_{ij}$ with direction $\theta_j$. If every weight is zero, the unshrunk weights $\hat s_j$ are used. By Proposition~\ref{prop:tau}, $\tau_k$ bounds one null standard deviation of the shot mean of the signed evidence, so statistics whose apparent separation is within the noise of $k$ shots receive no weight, while a statistic with a real margin above $\tau_k$ keeps its weight with probability approaching one exponentially fast. The threshold is a per-statistic noise floor; it does not control how many of the $9+2p$ statistics are retained by chance, which Section~\ref{sec:null} measures. The gate at $k=3$ reflects the same caution, since for $k\le2$, $\tau_k\ge0.20$ and a single shot lets a statistic without signal pass with probability $0.42$; the specific cut-off was chosen in the last development round, and Section~\ref{sec:sens} reports the alternatives.

\begin{algorithm}[!ht]
\caption{Few-shot direction calibration (FDC)}\label{alg:fdc}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require graph $(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{X})$; labelled anomalies $\mathcal{S}$, $|\mathcal{S}|=k$
\Ensure anomaly scores $s_i$ for all nodes
\State compute relational statistics $t_{i1},\dots,t_{i9}$, ranks $r_{ij}$, $\bar r_{ij}$ and masks $M_{ij}$ (Section~\ref{sec:detector})
\State compute $\mathbf{Z}$ and attribute statistics $z_{il}$ and $\frac{1}{d_i}\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}_i}z_{ul}$; their graph-wide ranks
\For{each statistic $j$}
  \State $\hat\mu^{\uparrow}_j,\hat\mu^{\downarrow}_j,\hat\mu^{\leftrightarrow}_j\gets$ Eq.~\eqref{eq:sep}; $\theta_j\gets$ arg max; $\hat s_j\gets\max(0,\hat\mu^{\theta_j}_j-\tfrac12)$
\EndFor
\If{$k<3$}
  \State $s_i\gets$ Eq.~\eqref{eq:fusion} on relational statistics with directions $\theta_j$ and weights $\omega_{ij}\hat s_j$ \Comment{FDC-R}
\Else
  \State $w_j\gets\max(0,\hat s_j-1/\sqrt{12k})$; if all $w_j=0$ then $w_j\gets\hat s_j$
  \State $s_i\gets$ Eq.~\eqref{eq:fdc} over all relational and attribute statistics
\EndIf
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{Cost.} The statistics are computed once per graph and do not depend on the labels. Their cost is that of the base detector, $O(|\mathcal{E}|d+\sum_u d_u^2)$ sparse operations with bounded memory, plus one truncated decomposition of the features. Calibration only averages $k$ precomputed ranks per statistic and forms a weighted mean, $O((9+2p)(k+n))$. The total cost of a first run is thus dominated by the label-independent preprocessing, which is not cheaper than training the official GDN on most graphs (Section~\ref{sec:runtime}); the advantage is that adding, removing or correcting labelled anomalies afterwards costs a fraction of a second.

\section{Experimental setup}\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Graphs.} Table~\ref{tab:datasets} lists the 20 graphs. Sixteen were used during development; four (Coauthor-CS and Amazon-Photo with injected anomalies, Books and Enron with organic anomalies) were held out and used once, for the confirmatory test of the frozen method. The held-out graphs are not untouched by the wider research process. In the earlier label-free rule study (Section~\ref{sec:rq4}) their labels were read once, to evaluate the frozen consensus rule, and the per-statistic diagnostic of Fig.~\ref{fig:diag} includes them. They were not used in any of the three development rounds of FDC, in choosing its statistics, or in the go/no-go and selection rules, and their labels were stored apart from the development labels. Only two of them contain organic anomalies, and Enron, with five anomalies, admits only $k=1$. Injected-anomaly graphs follow the conventional structural and contextual injection \citep{ding2019deep,liu2021cola,xu2022contrastive}; organic graphs follow the zero-shot protocols of UNPrompt and AnomalyGFM \citep{niu2025unprompt,qiao2025anomalygfm} and the sources cited there \citep{kumar2019predicting,mcauley2013amateurs,dou2020enhancing,sanchez2013statistical,zhao2020error,platonov2023critical,rayana2015collective,shchur2018pitfalls}. Two benchmarks exist in incompatible versions; we use the Weibo file distributed with ARC. Appendix~\ref{app:data} identifies every file and describes the preprocessing and anomaly injection.

\paragraph{Supervision.} For each graph, shot size $k\in\{1,3,5,10\}$ and seed in $\{11,23,37,53,71\}$, $k$ anomalies are drawn uniformly without replacement from the anomalous nodes with a seeded generator; no normal node is labelled. A combination is run only if $k$ is at most half the number of anomalies, which excludes Disney (6 anomalies) at $k\ge5$ and Enron (5 anomalies) at $k\ge3$. All methods receive identical shots. Metrics are computed on all nodes except the shots and averaged over seeds: AUROC, average precision (AP), AP normalised by the anomaly rate $\pi'$ of the evaluated nodes, $\mathrm{nAP}=(\mathrm{AP}-\pi')/(1-\pi')$, which is 0 for random ranking on every graph, and R-precision, the precision among the $K$ highest-scored nodes with $K$ the number of evaluated anomalies (equal to Recall@$K$). The main comparison uses the five seeds above for every method. For the revision analyses (Sections~\ref{sec:null}--\ref{sec:light}) FDC, FDC-R, GDN and the lightweight baselines were also run with 15 further seeds (101--115), 20 in total; BWGNN, which needed a separate machine, was run with the original five.

\paragraph{Baselines.} We use the official code of two methods that learn from labelled anomalies. GDN \citep{ding2021few} is taken from the Meta-GDN repository (commit \texttt{426516b}) with its SGC encoder, deviation loss, optimiser and training loop unchanged; each epoch trains on the $k$ labelled anomalies and $k$ unlabelled nodes, as in the official script. BWGNN \citep{tang2022rethinking} is taken from its official repository (commit \texttt{de0631f}), whose model file is downloaded and checked byte for byte before use; it is trained with the official loss and optimiser, with the labelled anomalies as positives and all other nodes as negatives. Neither few-shot setting has a labelled validation set, so the primary variant of each baseline uses its last epoch. We also report each baseline with model selection on a labelled validation set of 20\% of the non-shot nodes, as in the official scripts (marked $^{\dagger}$). This variant sees far more labels than any other method and is reported as an optimistic reference. Meta-GDN is not run, because it needs labelled auxiliary graphs that share the target's feature space. Treating unlabelled nodes as negatives, as both baselines do, contaminates the negative class with the unlabelled anomalies; this is the standard positive--unlabelled approximation \citep{elkan2008learning,bekker2020learning} and affects the baselines more than FDC, which never fits a classifier.

\paragraph{Lightweight baselines.} To test whether FDC's gains come from its calibration or simply from using labelled anomalies, we added four training-free baselines that receive the same $k$ anomalies: the maximum and the mean cosine similarity of each node to the shots in FDC's attribute space $[\mathbf{Z}, \text{neighbour mean of }\mathbf{Z}]$ (ShotSim-max, ShotSim-centroid), a positive--unlabelled logistic regression on the same features with balanced class weights \citep{elkan2008learning}, and the single statistic with the largest estimated separation, oriented by the shots (BestSingleStat).

\paragraph{Methods not compared under equal supervision.} ARC and AnomalyGFM use labelled \emph{normal} nodes in their few-shot modes, and UNPrompt, FreeGAD and NeighborDiv are zero-shot; none of them can use labelled anomalies, so a comparison with them would measure the supervision rather than the method. Section~\ref{sec:rq5} reports the normal-shot comparison of the base detector with ARC and AnomalyGFM. BWGNN was run on a separate Windows machine with the official CPU code and DGL 2.2.1; a check run on Cora reproduced, to all printed digits, the values of an independent implementation of the same graph operations on the development machine.

\paragraph{Computing environment.} All experiments except BWGNN ran in one Linux container (Ubuntu 24.04) with two virtual CPU cores of an Intel Xeon processor at 2.10\,GHz, 8\,GB of memory and no GPU, using Python 3.13, NumPy 2.5, SciPy 1.18, scikit-learn 1.9 and PyTorch 2.7 (CPU). BWGNN, whose official code needs DGL, ran on a Windows laptop (16 logical cores, 16\,GB of memory, CPU only) with Python 3.11, PyTorch 2.3 and DGL 2.2.1.

\paragraph{Development and freezing.} FDC was developed in three rounds on the development graphs, each with a protocol written and hashed before it was run (Appendix~\ref{app:prereg}). Round~1 tested relational-only calibration against a pre-specified go/no-go rule. Round~2 added attribute statistics in three pre-specified variants and a selection rule that also required the injected-graph mean to fall by no more than 0.02; the best variant failed that condition and was not adopted. Round~3 tested two variants aimed at that failure, and the $k$-gated variant, FDC, passed. The code and protocols were then hashed into a freeze record before any held-out label was read, and a confirmatory protocol fixed three claims for the held-out test: (C1) the mean AUROC of FDC is at least that of the better baseline per combination minus 0.01; (C2) FDC beats the better baseline in at least half of the combinations; (C3) FDC is at least as good as FDC-R. The SHA-256 hashes establish that the protocols and code were not changed after hashing, but not when they were written; the commits in the public repository are timestamped only from the date of upload. A registry with independent timestamps, such as OSF, would close this gap and will be used for future work.

\section{Results}\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Development graphs}\label{sec:devres}

Table~\ref{tab:main} and Fig.~\ref{fig:k} summarise the development results. With one labelled anomaly FDC (which is then FDC-R) reaches a mean AUROC of 0.680, against 0.544 for GDN and 0.490 for BWGNN. The gap widens with $k$: with ten labelled anomalies FDC reaches 0.800, against 0.645 and 0.527. FDC beats the better of the two baselines on 11--12 graphs at every $k$. Its AP is higher still in relative terms (0.387 at $k=10$, against 0.238 for GDN). Even the baselines with a labelled validation set stay below FDC from $k=3$ onwards, and GDN$^{\dagger}$ ties it at $k=1$ (0.682 against 0.680).

\subsection{Confirmatory test on held-out graphs}\label{sec:heldout}

Table~\ref{tab:heldout} reports the held-out test, run once with the frozen method. All three confirmatory claims hold. These claims were stated over the 13 (graph, $k$) combinations; since the combinations come from only four graphs, Section~\ref{sec:signif} assesses them at the graph level. FDC's mean AUROC is 0.723, against 0.546 for the better baseline per combination (C1); it beats both baselines in all 13 combinations (C2); and it exceeds FDC-R (0.681; C3). It also beats the baselines with a labelled validation set in 9 of 13 combinations. Two results qualify this. First, FDC's mean AP on the held-out graphs (0.225) is below FDC-R's (0.252), although its AUROC is higher; AP was not among the confirmatory claims, and Section~\ref{sec:light} examines it with further metrics and seeds. Second, on Coauthor-CS the attribute statistics slightly lower AUROC at $k\ge3$ (for example 0.939 against 0.963 at $k=3$). With a single labelled anomaly, Books is close to random for every method and Amazon-Photo stays below 0.61, which is what Theorem~\ref{thm:anomaly} predicts when the margins of the statistics are small relative to one shot.

\subsection{Statistical significance at the graph level}\label{sec:signif}

The runs within one graph share its nodes, edges and anomalies, so combinations of the same graph at different $k$ and seeds are not independent observations. We therefore take the graph as the unit of analysis (Table~\ref{tab:graphlevel}). For each graph, the effect is the mean difference between FDC and the comparison method over its paired $(k,\text{seed})$ runs. On the four held-out graphs we use the exact one-sided sign test over graphs, and on the 16 development graphs the one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test \citep{wilcoxon1945individual,demsar2006statistical}. The 95\% intervals come from a hierarchical bootstrap that resamples graphs and then seeds within each graph (10{,}000 replicates).

On the held-out graphs FDC has the higher AUROC on all four graphs against each of the four baselines. With four graphs, however, the smallest attainable sign-test $p$-value is $2^{-4}=0.0625$, so the held-out test cannot reach conventional significance at the graph level, whatever the effect. What it does show is an effect whose bootstrap interval excludes zero: $+0.174$ [0.072, 0.323] against GDN, $+0.218$ [0.085, 0.434] against BWGNN, and $+0.077$ [0.013, 0.169] against GDN with a labelled validation set. On the development graphs the differences against the last-epoch baselines are significant ($p\le0.0004$), and so is the difference against BWGNN$^{\dagger}$ ($p=0.0065$); against GDN$^{\dagger}$ it is not ($+0.035$, $p=0.072$). For AP the held-out evidence is weaker: FDC is ahead of BWGNN on three of the four graphs and its interval includes zero. FDC is not significantly better than FDC-R on the held-out graphs in either metric. We regard the held-out test as a pre-specified check that the frozen method transfers, not as a significance test with adequate power. Tests over (graph, $k$) combinations would treat correlated runs of the same graph as independent and overstate the evidence, and we do not use them.

\subsection{Ablation and development history}\label{sec:ablation}

Table~\ref{tab:ablation} lists every variant evaluated during development, in the order in which the rounds were run. Calibrating directions from the shots is the largest single gain (0.651 to 0.717 mean AUROC), and weighting by the estimated separation adds a further 0.010. Pooling attribute statistics helps organic graphs substantially (0.630 to 0.684) but hurts injected graphs and $k=1$; the null-shrinkage threshold recovers part of the injected loss, and sparse top-8 selection does not help. Gating the attribute statistics by $k$ keeps the organic gain and the $k=1$ performance of FDC-R. Because these variants were chosen on the development graphs, their differences should be read as development evidence; the held-out test of Section~\ref{sec:heldout} is the unbiased estimate of the final method.

\subsection{Lightweight baselines, further seeds and further metrics}\label{sec:light}

The comparison so far uses five seeds per combination and two trained baselines. Table~\ref{tab:light} adds 15 seeds (20 in total) and four training-free baselines that use the same $k$ labelled anomalies (Section~\ref{sec:setup}), and reports normalised AP and R-precision besides AUROC. All entries are means over graphs of per-graph means over $k$ and seeds, so each graph counts once. FDC's AUROC with 20 seeds (0.741 on the development graphs and 0.715 on the held-out graphs) is close to its five-seed values under the same aggregation (0.741 and 0.710).

Using the shots alone does not explain FDC's results. Similarity to the shots in FDC's own attribute space and a positive--unlabelled logistic regression on the same features reach development AUROC of 0.57--0.62, and the best single oriented statistic reaches 0.662. FDC is ahead of the single best statistic on all 16 development graphs in AUROC and on 15 in nAP (Wilcoxon $p<10^{-4}$ for both), so combining calibrated statistics adds to choosing one. With 20 seeds the official GDN reaches 0.588 on the development graphs and 0.533 on the held-out graphs, and its first five seeds reproduce the main comparison exactly. FDC is ahead of it in AUROC on 14 of 16 development graphs ($p=0.0002$; in nAP on 11, $p=0.033$) and in both metrics on all four held-out graphs. GDN with a labelled validation set comes closest on the development graphs (0.711; FDC ahead on 10 of 16, $p=0.12$), but its held-out nAP stays near zero (0.013).

The held-out graphs qualify this in the ranking metrics (Table~\ref{tab:heldoutmetrics}). FDC has the highest held-out AUROC of all methods, but its mean nAP (0.167) and R-precision (0.184) are below those of FDC-R (0.184, 0.190) and of the single best statistic (0.199, 0.227). The difference comes almost entirely from Coauthor-CS, where one relational statistic separates the injected anomalies very well (nAP 0.718) and pooling it with weaker attribute statistics dilutes the top of the ranking (0.572); on Books FDC has the highest nAP and on Enron it ties with FDC-R, while on Amazon-Photo BWGNN has the highest nAP (0.120) although its AUROC is only 0.546. FDC therefore improves the ranking as a whole more reliably than the precision among the highest-ranked nodes, and when one statistic dominates, pooling can cost precision at the top. Section~\ref{sec:sens} shows that a stricter weight threshold reduces this cost.

\subsection{Null experiment: how many statistics pass the threshold by chance}\label{sec:null}

The threshold $\tau_k=1/\sqrt{12k}$ is a per-statistic noise floor (Proposition~\ref{prop:tau}); it does not control the number of statistics retained when many are tested. To measure that number we replaced the $k$ labelled anomalies by $k$ nodes drawn uniformly at random, ran FDC unchanged, and counted the statistics with positive weight (Table~\ref{tab:null}; the $k$-gate is disabled here so that all statistics are counted at every $k$). With random shots about 42\% of the statistics are retained at every $k$, against 44--54\% with real shots. The threshold therefore removes most of the noise-level separations but by no means all, and the number of retained statistics is not by itself evidence of signal. What matters is how those statistics are combined. With random shots the resulting AUROC is 0.49--0.53 on average and between 0.47 and 0.58 on every graph, so the statistics retained by chance do not produce a spurious detector: their directions and weights are random and largely cancel. The two graphs above 0.55, Facebook (0.578) and Amazon-all (0.567), are graphs on which even the fixed directions detect the anomalies well (AUROC 0.876 and 0.760 at $k=10$), so a random orientation still finds part of the signal; these values remain far below FDC with real shots (0.972 and 0.905).

\subsection{Sensitivity to the threshold, the gate and the attribute dimension}\label{sec:sens}

The threshold multiplier ($\tau_k=c/\sqrt{12k}$, $c=1$ in FDC), the gate ($k\ge3$) and the attribute dimension ($p=16$) were fixed during development. Table~\ref{tab:sens} varies each of them with the others at their frozen values. AUROC changes little: over $c\in[0,2]$ it stays within 0.730--0.741 on the development graphs and 0.709--0.715 on the held-out graphs, and over the gate and $p$, short of dropping the attribute statistics altogether, within 0.701--0.741. FDC's frozen settings are the best of those tried in development AUROC, as expected for settings chosen on those graphs, and no alternative improves the held-out AUROC. The threshold matters more for nAP on the held-out graphs: removing it ($c=0$) lowers nAP from 0.167 to 0.130, and a stricter threshold ($c=2$) raises it to 0.196, at a cost of 0.011 development AUROC. This is the trade-off of Section~\ref{sec:light}: fewer weakly weighted statistics preserve precision at the top of the ranking when one statistic dominates. We keep the frozen $c=1$, because changing it after seeing the held-out results would void the confirmatory test, and report $c$ as a parameter that users concerned with top-ranked precision may raise.

The contextual statistics subsample $q=32$ neighbours and $L=128$ neighbour pairs per node. On seven development graphs (Amazon, BlogCatalog, CiteSeer, Cora, Tolokers, Weibo and YelpChi) we recomputed the statistics with $(q,L)$ halved and doubled (Table~\ref{tab:qL}). Mean AUROC changes by at most 0.001 and no per-graph mean changes by more than 0.006; the sampling budgets have no practical effect.

\subsection{Runtime}\label{sec:runtime}

Table~\ref{tab:runtime} reports wall-clock times for one run at the largest valid $k$, measured in the computing environment of Section~\ref{sec:setup} with two CPU threads. Both methods are timed from the graph held in memory: loading the file from disk (at most 0.9\,s) is excluded from both, and an untimed warm-up run absorbs PyTorch's one-off initialisation. For FDC the time is dominated by the label-independent preprocessing, from 0.07\,s on Disney to 82\,s on Amazon-all ($4.4\times10^6$ edges); calibration with the labelled anomalies takes at most 0.20\,s on any graph. The official GDN, a linear model on precomputed propagated features, is faster on 19 of the 20 graphs. The practical advantage of FDC is therefore not the speed of a single run: it needs no training, and once the preprocessing is done, adding or correcting labelled anomalies costs a fraction of a second.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{What the theory explains.} The results follow the asymmetry of Section~\ref{sec:theory}. Unlabelled data cannot orient a statistic (Theorem~\ref{thm:nonid}), which is why no label-free rule transferred. Labelled normal nodes look like the graph as a whole when anomalies are rare (Theorem~\ref{thm:normal}), which is why normal-shot rules stayed near chance. Labelled anomalies identify the direction at an exponential rate in $k$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:anomaly}), which is why FDC improves steadily with $k$ while its error on statistics with large margins vanishes. The observed direction errors stay within the bounds in every case (Table~\ref{tab:bound}).

\paragraph{Why the baselines struggle.} GDN and BWGNN learn a scoring function from the labelled anomalies, with all other nodes treated as normal. With one to ten positives, that function is easily fitted to features of the particular shots; BWGNN's last-epoch AUROC is below 0.5 on most graphs. FDC learns far less: one direction and one weight per statistic, each estimated by an average of $k$ bounded numbers. This low-variance estimate is what makes few shots sufficient, and it is also what limits FDC when no statistic carries the anomaly signal, as on Questions and Tolokers.

\paragraph{Implications for few-shot evaluation.} Generalist detectors are usually evaluated with a few labelled normal nodes. Our results suggest that, for detectors built on statistics, a few labelled anomalies are far more informative, and that few-shot protocols should include them. They also suggest that the orientation of each statistic should be reported as an explicit assumption of any training-free detector.

\paragraph{Pooling and precision at the top.} FDC pools every statistic whose estimated separation exceeds the noise floor. This raises AUROC on most graphs, since several moderately informative statistics rank the bulk of the anomalies better than any one of them, but it can dilute a single dominant statistic among the highest-ranked nodes, as on Coauthor-CS (Section~\ref{sec:light}). The null experiment shows why the threshold alone cannot prevent this: about two in five statistics pass it by chance. A stricter threshold, or an explicit correction for the number of statistics tested, would favour top-ranked precision; we did not adopt either after the held-out test, to keep that test confirmatory.

\paragraph{Limitations.} FDC is built on one family of statistics; it inherits their blind spots, and on graphs without informative statistics (Reddit, Questions) every method stays close to random. The held-out test contains four graphs, so at the graph level it can show a consistent effect with bootstrap intervals but cannot reach conventional significance; only two of the graphs have organic anomalies, and Enron admits only $k=1$. The held-out graphs were not used in developing FDC, but their labels had been read once before, in the label-free rule study and the diagnostic of Fig.~\ref{fig:diag}. The protocol hashes establish that files were not changed after hashing, not when they were written. FDC's held-out nAP and R-precision are below those of FDC-R and of the best single statistic, and its threshold and gate were chosen on the development graphs. The baselines were run with their official settings, without tuning, and treat unlabelled nodes as negatives; with a labelled validation set they improve, and we report that variant throughout. Meta-GDN, which needs labelled auxiliary graphs in the same feature space, was not compared, and recent semi-supervised and positive--unlabelled detectors beyond GDN, BWGNN and the lightweight baselines were not run. BWGNN was run with five seeds and without R-precision. Finally, FDC is not faster than GDN for a single run.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Training-free graph anomaly detectors depend on a choice that unlabelled data cannot make: which tail of each statistic is anomalous. We proved that labelled normal nodes barely help with this choice when anomalies are rare, and that a few labelled anomalies settle it at an exponential rate. Few-shot direction calibration turns this into a method with no trainable parameters. Evaluated against the official GDN and BWGNN under identical supervision, with protocols fixed in advance and a held-out confirmatory test, it was better on most development graphs, with graph-level significance, and had the higher AUROC on all four held-out graphs. It also outperformed the single best calibrated statistic and shot-similarity baselines, and was insensitive to its sampling and threshold settings in AUROC, although on one held-out graph pooling cost precision at the top of the ranking. The results argue for treating orientation as an explicit, testable part of statistic-based detectors and for including labelled anomalies in few-shot evaluation.

\section{Proofs}\label{app:proofs}

Throughout, $c(i,l) = \mathbb{1}[t_l < t_i] + \tfrac12\mathbb{1}[t_l = t_i]$, so that $c(i,l) + c(l,i) = 1$ and $c(i,i) = \tfrac12$.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:sign}]
By \eqref{eq:rankpos}, $U_i = \frac1n\sum_{l\in V} c(i,l)$. Splitting the inner sum into anomalies and normal nodes,
\[
m\,\mu = \sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}} U_i
= \frac1n\Big(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}}\sum_{l\in\mathcal{A}} c(i,l) + \sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}}\sum_{l\in\mathcal{N}} c(i,l)\Big)
= \frac1n\Big(\frac{m^2}{2} + m(n-m)\,\mathrm{AUC}\Big),
\]
because the $m^2$ ordered pairs within $\mathcal{A}$ split into pairs $(i,l),(l,i)$ contributing $1$ each and diagonal terms contributing $\tfrac12$ each, for a total of $m^2/2$. Dividing by $m$ gives $\mu = \pi/2 + (1-\pi)\,\mathrm{AUC}$, that is, $\mu - \tfrac12 = (1-\pi)(\mathrm{AUC} - \tfrac12)$. Since $1 - \pi > 0$, $\mu - \tfrac12$ and $\mathrm{AUC} - \tfrac12$ have the same sign.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:nonid}]
With distinct values, every node in $\mathcal{A}_\uparrow$ has a larger value than every node outside it, so labelling $\mathcal{A}_\uparrow$ as anomalous gives $\mathrm{AUC} = 1$; symmetrically, labelling $\mathcal{A}_\downarrow$ gives $\mathrm{AUC} = 0$. Both labellings have $m$ anomalies. A label-free rule $\phi$ sees the same input under both, so $p = \Pr[\phi = \text{upper}]$ is the same. Its error is $1 - p$ under the first labelling and $p$ under the second, and $\max(1-p,\,p) \ge \tfrac12$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:normal}]
Let $M = V \setminus (\mathcal{A}_\uparrow \cup \mathcal{A}_\downarrow)$, $|M| = n - 2m \ge m'$. Under the first labelling the normal nodes are $M \cup \mathcal{A}_\downarrow$; under the second they are $M \cup \mathcal{A}_\uparrow$. Both sets have $n - m$ elements. Let $S$ be the set of $m'$ revealed normal nodes and $E$ the event $S \subseteq M$. Under either labelling,
\[
\Pr[E] = \binom{n-2m}{m'}\Big/\binom{n-m}{m'} = \prod_{i=0}^{m'-1}\frac{n-2m-i}{n-m-i} = q,
\]
and conditionally on $E$, $S$ is a uniform $m'$-subset of $M$ under both labellings. Hence, on $E$, the observed data $(G, S)$ have the same distribution under both labellings, and so does the output of any rule $\phi$. Write $p_E = \Pr[\phi = \text{upper} \mid E]$. Then
\[
\Pr_{\uparrow}[\text{error}] + \Pr_{\downarrow}[\text{error}]
\;\ge\; q\,(1 - p_E) + q\,p_E \;=\; q,
\]
so the larger of the two errors is at least $q/2$. Each factor of the product is at least its last factor, which gives $q \ge \big((n-2m-m'+1)/(n-m-m'+1)\big)^{m'} = \big(1 - m/(n-m-m'+1)\big)^{m'}$. For $m' \ll n$ this is approximately $\big(1-\pi/(1-\pi)\big)^{m'} \approx \exp(-m'\pi/(1-\pi))$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:anomaly}]
Assume the upper tail is anomalous, so $\mu = \tfrac12 + \Delta$; the other case is symmetric. The rule errs only if $\hat\mu \le \tfrac12$, that is, if $\hat\mu - \mu \le -\Delta$. The shots are drawn without replacement from the finite population $\{U_i : i \in \mathcal{A}\}$, whose values lie in $(0,1)$ and have mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. \citet{hoeffding1963probability}, Theorem~4, shows that for every continuous convex function $f$, $\mathbb{E} f(\sum_s U_{a_s})$ under sampling without replacement is at most its value under sampling with replacement. Every exponential-moment (Chernoff) bound for independent draws therefore also holds here. Hoeffding's inequality for independent variables with range $1$ gives $\Pr[\hat\mu - \mu \le -\Delta] \le \exp(-2k\Delta^2)$. Bernstein's inequality, with variance $\sigma^2$ and $|U_{a_s} - \mu| \le 1$, gives $\Pr[\hat\mu - \mu \le -\Delta] \le \exp\!\big(-k\Delta^2 / (2\sigma^2 + 2\Delta/3)\big)$. Both are derived from exponential moments, so both apply.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:k}]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:anomaly} and a union bound over the $J$ statistics, the probability that at least one direction is wrong is at most $J\exp(-2k\Delta_{\min}^2)$. This is at most $\varepsilon$ when $k \ge \ln(J/\varepsilon)/(2\Delta_{\min}^2)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:three}]
For a candidate $t \ne t^*$, let $D_s = e^{t}_{a_s} - e^{t^*}_{a_s} \in [-1,1]$ be the difference of the two evidences of shot $s$. Its population mean over $\mathcal{A}$ is $-g_t$. Candidate $t$ is chosen over $t^*$ only if the shot mean of $D_s$ is at least $0$, that is, at least $g_t$ above its mean. By Hoeffding's inequality for variables with range $2$, valid under sampling without replacement as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:anomaly}, this has probability at most $\exp(-2k g_t^2/4) = \exp(-k g_t^2/2)$. A union bound over the other two candidates gives the claim. For the two signed tails, $e^{\uparrow} - e^{\downarrow} = 2U - 1$, so $g = 2\Delta$ and the bound is $\exp(-2k\Delta^2)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:tau}]
(a) The rank positions $U_i$ are midranks divided by $n$. Their mean over all nodes is exactly $\tfrac12$ with or without ties, because midranks always sum to $n(n+1)/2$. Without ties their variance is $(n^2-1)/(12n^2) < 1/12$; ties replace the ranks of each tied group by the group's mean rank, which can only lower the variance (the standard tie correction subtracts $\sum_g (t_g^3 - t_g)/(12n^3)$, with $t_g$ the size of tied group $g$). The lower evidence is $1-U$ and has the same mean and variance. If the $k$ shots are a uniform random sample of nodes, the shot mean has expectation $\tfrac12$ and variance at most $1/(12k)$; sampling without replacement multiplies this by $(n-k)/(n-1) \le 1$.

(b) The two-sided evidence is $|r| = |2U-1|$. For distinct values its mean is $\tfrac12$ for even $n$ and $\tfrac12 - 1/(2n^2)$ for odd $n$. Ties replace the values of $U$ within a tied group by their average; since $u \mapsto |2u-1|$ is convex, Jensen's inequality shows that this cannot increase the group's mean two-sided evidence, so $m_j \le \tfrac12$ in general and $m_j$ decreases with heavier ties. Because $|r| \in [0,1]$, its variance is at most $\tfrac14$. Ties can increase it above $\tfrac1{12}$: for three equal groups of sizes $\tfrac n4, \tfrac n2, \tfrac n4$, $|r|$ takes the values $0.75, 0, 0.75$, so $m_j = 0.375$ and $\sigma_j^2 = 0.141$. The shot mean has expectation $m_j$ and variance at most $\sigma_j^2/k$.

(c) Let statistic $j$ have margin $\Delta_j > \tau_k$, and say its upper tail is anomalous. The estimated separation of the chosen tail is at least that of the upper tail, $\hat s_j \ge \hat\mu - \tfrac12$. The weight is zero only if $\hat s_j \le \tau_k$, which implies $\hat\mu - \mu \le -(\Delta_j - \tau_k)$. By the Hoeffding step in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:anomaly}, this has probability at most $\exp(-2k(\Delta_j - \tau_k)^2)$.
\end{proof}

\section{Benchmark files, preprocessing and anomaly injection}\label{app:data}
\setcounter{table}{0}

Table~\ref{tab:files} identifies every benchmark file: its name, the repository and commit from which it was obtained, and the first 12 hexadecimal digits of its SHA-256 hash; \texttt{data/download\_data.py} in the code repository downloads the files and checks the hashes. Each file is read as distributed. The adjacency matrix is symmetrised ($\mathbf{A}\leftarrow\max(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{A}^{\top})$), self-loops are removed and edge weights are set to 1; labels are binarised (any non-zero label is an anomaly); features are read as stored and then preprocessed as in Section~\ref{sec:detector} (median imputation of non-finite entries, removal of constant columns, column standardisation and row normalisation). Edge counts in Table~\ref{tab:datasets} are undirected edges after this cleaning. No node or edge is removed.

We did not inject anomalies ourselves. The injected-anomaly files follow the protocol of \citet{ding2019deep}, used by CoLA and ARC \citep{liu2021cola,liu2024arc}: structural anomalies are $m$ cliques of 15 nodes formed by adding edges among randomly chosen nodes, and an equal number of contextual anomalies have their attributes replaced by those of the most distant of 50 randomly chosen nodes. We checked the structural part in each file: the anomalous nodes contain exactly the $m$ cliques of 15 nodes listed in Table~\ref{tab:files}, and the files that store separate structural and contextual labels contain 15$m$ of each. ACM stores no per-type labels and has 597 anomalies for 20 cliques. The Facebook file is an exception: it contains no clique of five or more anomalous nodes, and its 25 anomalies come from \citet{xu2022contrastive}, so it does not follow the clique protocol. It was grouped with the injected graphs in the round-1 protocol, as in the earlier study, and we keep that grouping because the round-2 and round-3 selection rules were applied with it. The grouping matters for one decision. With Facebook counted as organic, FDC's injected-graph mean would be 0.0215 below that of FDC-R in round 3, just outside the pre-specified tolerance of 0.02, instead of 0.0137; the overall means, which do not depend on the grouping, are unchanged. Organic-anomaly files are used with the labels supplied by their sources.
